extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers (undergraduate, graduate, and professional researchers across fields)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting, drafting, and revising research projects and formal research reports so they address significant problems, persuade readers, and follow disciplinary forms and ethical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching problem significance to effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide you through the complexities of turning a topic or question into a research problem whose significance matches the effort that you put into solving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a problem with a significance that justifies the work; transform interests into focused problems readers will think worth posing and solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize and draft a report that justifies the effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Help you organize and draft a report that justifies the effort of the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a plan for the report that lets readers find and judge the central claim and evidence; use standard forms/genres to help readers locate key information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read your report as your readers will
rubrics_metrics.description: Show you how to read your report as your readers will so that you can revise it into one that they will read with understanding and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly imagine readers' questions and reservations; revise from their perspective to improve clarity, organization, and persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn a vague interest into a significant research problem
rubrics_metrics.description: How to turn a vague interest into a problem readers think is worth posing and solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move from an interest to a topic, to a focused topic, to questions, and then into a problem whose significance you can demonstrate; use framing to show why the problem matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build an argument that motivates readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an argument that motivates readers to take your claim seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat argument as a conversation with readers: state claim, supply reasons and evidence, warrant their relevance, anticipate objections, and thicken ethos to increase credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reservations and respond appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and respond to anticipated questions and objections from thoughtful but critical readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which objections to acknowledge, frame responses as subordinate arguments, use appropriate vocabulary of acknowledgment and response, and select predictable disagreements to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create introductions and conclusions that answer 'So what?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an introduction and conclusion that answer the reader's question: So what?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductions should establish common ground, state the problem, and state your response; conclusions should state the significance and possible next steps; set the right pace and opening/closing words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two kinds of plans (research and draft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced researchers create two kinds of plans: one to guide the search (research plan) and a second to guide drafting (draft plan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep plans flexible; use a research plan to guide data gathering and a rough blueprint/outline to guide the first draft — change them as the project develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and imagine your reader's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Create roles for yourself and your readers and imagine your reader's role when composing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what readers already know, what they need to know, what questions they'll ask, and what standards they use; use checklists/quick tips to understand readers and adapt tone, form, and level of explanation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: From topics to research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn an interest into a topic and a topic into focused research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow broad interests stepwise; convert a focused topic into explicit questions that drive significance and method; use quick tips for finding topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: From questions to a research problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform questions into a research problem and distinguish practical from research problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the common structure of problems, assess costs and consequences, find good research problems, and learn to work with problems even when inexperienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and use three kinds of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how to use three kinds of sources (primary, secondary, tertiary) and the roles they play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use primary sources for original data, secondary sources for interpretation and models, and tertiary sources for orientation; use each kind strategically to define problems and plan arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate sources effectively (library and Internet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate sources through a library and on the Internet using appropriate tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use libraries, specialized indexes and databases, Google Scholar, and careful internet searches; distinguish reliable library-based online resources from less reliable web content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sources for relevance and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate sources for relevance to your question and for reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess currency, authority, agreement/disagreement across sources, and applicability to your problem; look beyond predictable sources and use people as primary sources where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record complete bibliographical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Record complete bibliographic data for every source you consult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture full citations when you first encounter a source to avoid errors later; use consistent citation styles and note-taking practices to support ethical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage sources actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage sources actively rather than passively accepting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read sources for arguments, evidence, and disagreements; use secondary sources to find problems and plan arguments; record what you find and manage research anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish evidence, reasons, and reports of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish evidence from reasons and from reports of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reasons to plan an argument, ensure evidence truly supports reasons, and avoid conflating a report of evidence with the evidence itself; evaluate sufficiency and reliability of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make and evaluate appropriate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what kind of claim you should make and evaluate its appropriateness and significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit, specific, and significant; evaluate claims for scope and contribution; use hedges and limiting conditions where needed; qualify claims to enhance credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble reasons and evidence to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reasons and evidence systematically to plan and present your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build complex arguments from simple ones, order reasons so they support the claim, show how each piece of evidence is relevant, and thicken the argument to create ethos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use warrants to connect reasons to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit the warrants that justify the relevance of your reasons to your claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand warrants (everyday and academic), test their reliability, know when to state them, and challenge others' warrants; use definitions and plausible instances to support warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and respond to alternatives and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what alternatives and objections to acknowledge and how to frame responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine readers' likely questions, present alternatives as subordinate arguments, choose which objections to include, and use three predictable disagreements as a guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan, draft, and revise (process guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan your report, draft in a way that suits you, and revise organization, argument, and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid common flawed planning approaches, use outlines/storyboards/road maps, draft using key words and comfortable methods, then revise thinking like a reader — revise frame, argument, organization, and paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting mechanics: quoting, paraphrasing, summarizing, and citing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote, paraphrase, and summarize appropriately and indicate citations clearly to avoid plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate quotations into your text, show readers how evidence is relevant, record bibliographic info, use standard citation styles (APA, MLA, Chicago), and guard against inadvertent plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against plagiarism and act ethically in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Take steps to avoid plagiarism and observe ethical responsibilities in research and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep careful notes distinguishing your ideas from sources', provide proper attribution, understand copyright and human-subjects ethics, and treat others' ideas as you would want yours treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate quantitative evidence visually and ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the most effective visual representation (table, chart, graph) and design it clearly and ethically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between visual and verbal representations, pick appropriate graphic types (bar, line, pie, histograms, scatterplots), design labels/legends/titles clearly, avoid misleading correlations, and follow ethical guidelines for visual data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the introduction and set the frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the common structure of introductions: establish common ground, state the problem, and state your response; set pace and provide road maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use working introductions, name key concepts, create road maps for readers, set expectations for scope and pace, and revise the frame as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise style for clarity: core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply stylistic principles to make writing clear: two primary principles, old-before-new, active vs passive, and complexity-last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge style for clarity, favor concrete over abstract, place old information before new, prefer active verbs unless passive is warranted, postpone complexity, and use 'spit and polish' editing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan organization with paragraphs, sections, and road maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan and revise the organization of the report down to paragraphs, sections, and subsections so readers can follow the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use storyboards, outlines, point-based or topic-based outlines, check paragraph unity/coherence, use headings and road maps, and let drafts cool before paraphrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use genre-appropriate forms to help readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt standard forms or genres appropriate to your audience (e.g., journalistic pyramid, IMRAD scientific form, audit report) to make it easy for readers to find needed information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within standard forms, writers can emphasize different ideas, but forms help readers locate the gist and specific issues; tailor organization to readers' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to remember, understand, and test thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Use writing as a tool to remember what you've read, to discover patterns and connections, and to test the quality of your ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write early and often during research; use notes and journals to compare sources, reveal contradictions, and see where arguments need strengthening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and evaluate graphical details (labels, legends, numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design tables and graphs with effective labels, legends, titles, and clear numbers to convey the intended rhetorical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanatory text, choose appropriate scales, avoid clutter, and align the visual with the argument you're making; be mindful of ethical presentation of quantitative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid three common but flawed planning approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid common flawed plans that derail drafting and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book warns against three unspecified common flawed plans (detailed in chapter 12) and suggests better planning strategies such as storyboarding and point-based outlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and revise warrants and the logic of your argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and test the logic of warrants connecting evidence and reasons to claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze warrants for plausibility and reliability, know when to state them explicitly, use supporting definitions and plausible instances, and be prepared to defend or challenge warrants in academic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical presentation of graphical and quantitative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate data ethically, avoiding misleading graphs and false correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidelines for ethical graphics (226-29), label clearly, avoid deceptive scales or selective data, and disclose methods and limitations when presenting quantitative evidence.
